title: Psychrometric Chart Explorer
description: Students will use (Bloom Level 3, Apply) a psychrometric chart to find the dew point and relative humidity of air at a given state, and will predict (Bloom Level 2, Understand) what happens to RH and dew point when the air is warmed or cooled.
creator: The Science of the Built Environment
author: Dan McCreary
subject: The Science of the Built Environment
chapter_title: Moisture, Air Movement, and Thermal Comfort

pedagogical.learningObjective: Use a psychrometric chart to find the dew point and relative humidity of air at a given state, and predict what happens to RH and dew point when the air is warmed or cooled.
recommendedUsage: Drag the orange dot, or use the Air temperature and Relative humidity sliders. The readout shows the temperature, humidity ratio, RH, and dew point.
Follow the dashed horizontal line from the dot to the left. Where it meets the dark blue saturation line is the dew point.
Press Warm 20°F and Cool 20°F. The dot moves along its horizontal line, so the humidity ratio and dew point stay the same while RH changes. Read the message below the chart.
Check Wall surface test and set the surface temperature. The marker turns red and the readout says Condensation when the surface is at or below the dew point.
Hover over any curve to read its RH.
activities: Warm-up (5 min): Students predict the dew point of 70°F air at 30 percent RH, then read it from the chart (about 37°F).
Explore (10 min): Students start with saturated air at -10°F and press Warm 20°F three times, recording the RH each time. They compare the result with the Chapter 4 example of dry winter air indoors.
Apply (10 min): With the surface test on, students raise the indoor RH from 20 to 50 percent at 70°F and find the surface temperatures that begin to condense at each RH.
assessment: Students explain in two sentences why warming air lowers its RH but does not change its dew point.
Students use the chart to decide whether a 45°F window pane will condense in 70°F air at 50 percent RH.
